extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of moral/observational essays; educated general public
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing short moral and satirical essays (Spectator-style): when to use first person, how to handle prefaces and self-disclosure, use of allegory/vision to teach morals, and habits to avoid in witty/epistolary pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid egotism / speaking of oneself indiscriminately
rubrics_metrics.description: Talking of himself generally proceeds from vanity; an ostentatious Man will rather relate a Blunder or an Absurdity he has committed, than be debarred from talking of his own dear Person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise every writer never to speak of himself, unless there be something very considerable in his Character. The passage cites Tully/Cicero, Montaigne, and authors of memoirs as exemplars of egotism; modern prefaces often savour strongly of egotism. Use self-reference sparingly to avoid vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person permitted in humorous/fictitious personae
rubrics_metrics.description: In Works of Humour, especially when a Man writes under a fictitious Personage, the talking of one's self may give some Diversion to the Publick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an exception to the general rule against self-disclosure: in comic or satirical pieces where a persona is adopted, first-person remarks can be entertaining and illuminating. Elsewhere, prefer restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use self-disclosure selectively to illuminate character or history
rubrics_metrics.description: Such Openings of the Heart give a Man a thorough Insight into his Personal Character, and illustrate several Passages in the History of his Life: besides that, there is some little Pleasure in discovering the Infirmity of a great Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a writer does choose to speak of himself, ensure it serves to reveal character or contextualise historical passages; self-revelation that informs the reader is tolerable and often valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivial prefatory details (where, why, who urged publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of our modern Prefaces savour very strongly of the Egotism. Every insignificant Author fancies it of Importance to the World, to know that he writ his Book in the Country, that he did it to pass away some of his idle Hours, that it was published at the Importunity of Friends, or that his natural Temper, Studies or Conversations, directed him to the Choice of his Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not burden a preface with irrelevant personal anecdotes or excuses — such information is of little value to the reader and often reads as vanity or self-justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pass off well-known jests or common wit as original
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one kind of Egotists ... who repeat as Sayings of their own ... several Jests which were made before they were born, and which every one who has conversed in the World has heard a hundred times over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid this absurdity, read collections (e.g., Oxford and Cambridge jests) and familiar sources so you do not inadvertently present stale material as your own—this preserves authorial credibility and humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use allegory/vision to teach moral lessons about human condition
rubrics_metrics.description: A vision (the Mountain of Miseries) and personifications (FANCY and PATIENCE) are used to show that people prefer their own hardships and that patience makes burdens more bearable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid allegory, personification, and concrete episodes (exchanges of misfortunes, contrasts between Fancy and Patience) to make moral points: show rather than merely assert that evils become tolerable by custom and that compassion and patience are virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirize social hypocrisy through concrete examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of doubled-tongued people (calling grief but soon smiling, saying 'sorry for your storm' and then not helping) and of courtly compliments (excessive apologies for trifles) illustrate social falseness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In satirical writing, rely on specific, often comic vignettes of behavior (false compliments, empty civility, polite falsehoods) to expose hypocrisy; make the social vice concrete and recognisable rather than abstract.
